bull_bear.body:
- Century-old brand: associated with India's mobility and industrial sectors since 1928, with 96 years of global brand history
- Pan-India distribution: a well-established network of depots, distributors, retail outlets and workshops giving widespread market access
- International footprint across more than 70 countries and five continents, which management describes as providing structural resilience and diversification against domestic cycles
- Portfolio premiumisation - 42% premium mix, with a stated shift into higher-value synthetic and high-performance products
- Manufacturing and R&D base: 5 ISO-accredited plants and 2 government-recognised R&D centres supporting OEM-specification products
- Group structure adding geography and capability: wholly owned overseas subsidiaries (Veedol International Limited, Veedol International FZCO, Veedol UK Limited), step-down Granville Oil & Chemicals Limited, and a 50% joint venture in ENEOS VCL India Private Limited

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Industry risk - competitive intensity and raw-material price fluctuation — The Company operates in a highly competitive lubricant market where fluctuation in raw material prices and changes in demand patterns can influence profitability, and economic downturns may dampen industrial activity and reduce lubricant consumption. Mitigated through index-based term contracts for crude procurement, supplier performance reviews, monitoring of competitor pricing, OEM movements and vehicle parc data, and a strong distribution network.
- Research and development risk — Inadequate or unsuccessful R&D can limit the ability to innovate and meet shifting market requirements, resulting in loss of competitiveness and market share. Mitigated by tracking API, ACEA and JASO category announcements, working with top additive manufacturers and maintaining OEM dialogue.
- Technology risk - failure to upgrade production and quality-control infrastructure — The lubricant industry keeps advancing production and quality-control systems; failure to upgrade promptly may lead to operational inefficiencies, higher production costs and impact on product quality and competitiveness.
- Credit risk on distributors and customers — Distributor and customer default, which may rise in an economic slowdown, affects cash flow. Managed through strict working-capital oversight, monthly sales and operations planning, analytical tools, internal funds and bank credit lines, and periodic review of internal financial controls.
- Inventory risk - obsolescence and working-capital lock-up — Excess stock can become obsolete as demand shifts, locking up working capital and raising storage costs. Managed through frequent stock checks, internal audits, alignment of inventory with production and delivery schedules and regular rebalancing of slow or non-moving stock.
- Foreign exchange risk from multi-geography operations — Currency movements influence both raw-material cost and realisation from export revenues, affecting overall financial performance; the Company monitors exposure and deploys hedging mechanisms where necessary.
- Cyber security and data privacy risk — Cyberattacks may lead to data breaches, system intrusions and disruption to business operations. Addressed via endpoint security and hardware firewalls across all operational locations, annual cybersecurity and VAPT audits, daily monitoring, and employee phishing simulation drills; cyber security is specifically covered by the Board-adopted Risk Management Plan.
- Climate change - regulatory, operational and reputational exposure — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative financial implications; mitigation is adoption of renewable energy, energy-efficiency improvement, environmental risk mapping and planned ESG advisory to build climate resilience into operations.
- Supply chain management risk — BRSR material issue flagged as a risk with negative financial implications - quality, compliance and continuity failures in the supply chain can disrupt operations and impact brand value; mitigated by quality- and compliance-based procurement, MSME supplier awareness sessions and preference for audited vendors.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Veedol manufactures and markets a wide range of automotive and industrial lubricants. The portfolio spans engine oils for passenger vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, commercial vehicles, tractors and off-highway equipment, together with gear oils, transmission fluids, coolants, brake oils, greases and a range of industrial and specialty lubricants, developed to meet evolving OEM specifications. Products reach customers through a pan-India network of depots, distributors, retail outlets and workshops and through exports to more than 70 countries; the Company operates 5 ISO-accredited manufacturing facilities and 2 government-recognised R&D centres, and holds a 50% stake in the ENEOS VCL India joint venture.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Automotive lubricants:** Two-wheeler Oils, Passenger Car Motor Oils, Commercial Vehicle Oils, Tractor Oils, Off-Highway Oils, EV Fluids, Gear and Transmission Oils, Automotive Fluids, Transmission Oils, Coolants, Greases, Vehicle care
- **Industrial lubricants:** Hydraulic Oils, Hydraulic and Circulation Oils, Heavy-Duty Hydraulic Oils, Steam Cylinder Oils, Mill Roll Oils, Thermic Fluids, Industrial Gear Oils, Pneumatic Tool Oils, Spindle Oils, Compressor Oils, Refrigeration Compressor Oils, Metal Working Fluids, Turbine Oils, Slideway Oil, Cardium Compounds
- **Specialities:** Lithium Based Greases, Lithium Complex Greases, Calcium Complex Greases, Calcium Sulphonate Complex Greases, Aluminium Complex Greases, Graphite Greases, Non-Soap Greases
- **OEM Oils:** OEM oils - lubricants specially formulated and approved by vehicle manufacturers to meet the precise requirements of their engines (no separate SKU list printed in this bundle)

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Premiumisation: repositioning away from the commodity segment towards premium, high-performance and synthetic lubricants, which management links to higher margins even where volumes lag
- Product development priority on high-performance premium lubricants, leveraging advanced R&D, sustainable formulations and cutting-edge technology, with the automotive and industrial focus on efficiency, extended equipment life and reduced environmental impact
- Sweat existing assets before expanding: the manufacturing strategy prioritises optimisation of existing infrastructure through operational excellence, improved planning and productivity enhancement initiatives before undertaking significant capacity expansion
- Reduce dependence on select high-volume plants in favour of greater regional manufacturing efficiency and more effective use of legacy infrastructure
- White-space market coverage: targeted expansion into underpenetrated and high-potential markets, appointing new channel partners and filling white-spot territories, supported by distributor restructuring in select regions
- Re-engaging the trade: re-establishing relationships with mechanics and independent workshops
- Distribution redesign: transition from a conventional distribution model to an integrated hub-and-spoke logistics framework built on four centralised regional hubs across a 32-depot network, with the V-Lakshya cost programme
- Integrated planning: institutionalisation of a formal Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) process plus MRP-based scheduling to improve forecast accuracy, production planning, inventory balance and working-capital efficiency
- Industrial lubricants repair rather than volume chase: improving customer quality, strengthening receivables discipline and improving portfolio profitability through selective rationalisation
- Quality and safety systems as an operating discipline: end-to-end quality control, real-time batch traceability, the V Suraksha safety initiative and V Excel packaging standards
- EV readiness: aligning product development to EV fluid development, advanced formulations and continuous innovation alongside the conventional ICE portfolio
- International platform: wholly owned overseas subsidiaries (Veedol International Limited, Veedol International FZCO, Veedol UK Limited) and the 50%-held ENEOS VCL India joint venture as contributors to consolidated performance
- Dividend is returned in instalments through the year: the 103rd AGM notice asks members to confirm the payment of first and second interim dividends and to declare a final dividend for the financial year ended 31st March, 2026. Remuneration is affirmed to be paid as per the Remuneration Policy for Directors, Key Managerial Personnel, Senior Management Personnel and other employees. None of the Directors or Key Managerial Personnel holds equity shares or convertible instruments in the Company. No dividend policy text, buyback, debt-reduction or reinvestment statement appears in the text routed to this domain.
- Climate action target: 25% reduction in total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2030
- Long-term target of attaining Net Zero emissions by 2050
- Improve overall energy efficiency by 25% by 2030 through plant-level optimisation initiatives
- Increase renewable energy to 25% of total energy consumption by 2030
- 25% reduction in water withdrawal by 2032; aspiration to become water positive by 2040
- Long-term goal of achieving Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) at operations
- Maintain 100% compliance with applicable hazardous waste management and disposal requirements
- Integrate 100% of identified ESG risks into the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework, and undertake a comprehensive ESG study in the coming financial year
- Maintain zero compliance breaches through governance processes and risk management systems
- Achieve an EcoVadis sustainability score of 70% or higher by 2030
- ISO 31000:2018 certification of the Enterprise Risk Management framework, with regular surveillance certifications
- All five plants - Faridabad, Howrah, Turbhe, Silvassa and Oragadam - certified under ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018
- Energy transition levers in place: onsite solar installations, wind energy investments, transition to cleaner fuels such as Piped Natural Gas, and plant-level energy monitoring systems
- Circular economy: increasing use of recycled packaging, exploring reusability of industrial waste streams and vendor collaboration on recycling
- Occupational health and safety managed to a zero-LTI track record, with regular health check-ups, mock drills and medical surveillance programmes
- Human rights embedded through contract clauses, grievance redressal, training and escalation procedures up to Managing Director level
- Skill development CSR spine: Veedol Auto Mechanic Academy (VAMA) at Chaibasa, Jharkhand achieving placement of over 75% of assessed candidates, and an EV maintenance and repair programme at Chandil, Jharkhand with placements at Mahindra's Adityapur facility
- Healthcare access through Mobile Medical Units run with SEVAMOB at Oragadam and Faridabad and with Sewa International across Haryana, Uttarakhand and Tripura
- Governance and grievance infrastructure: policies covering all nine NGRBC principles, Board-approved and translated into procedures, extended to value-chain partners, with a dedicated customer grievance portal and a published Grievance Redressal Policy
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Veedol's stated approach is to sweat existing assets rather than add capacity: the manufacturing strategy prioritises optimisation of existing infrastructure through operational excellence, improved planning and productivity enhancement initiatives before undertaking significant capacity expansion. The Company operates 5 ISO-accredited manufacturing facilities and 2 government-recognised R&D centres, with the footprint distributed across key regions of India for market coverage and service responsiveness. During FY 2025-26 the work was modernisation rather than greenfield: focused modernisation and operational improvement initiatives were undertaken at the Faridabad (Haryana) and Howrah (West Bengal) facilities to improve operational efficiency and asset utilisation, and dependence on select high-volume plants was reduced in favour of greater regional manufacturing efficiency and more effective use of legacy infrastructure. Capital expenditure described in the BRSR was capability rather than capacity: investment in advanced testing equipment (Rheometer, Quantum Tester, Four-Ball Tester and Salt Spray Tester) to support development of high-performance, fuel-efficient and low-emission lubricants, and development of products compatible with modern engine technologies including TGDI, GDI and low-viscosity requirements. No new plant, line or commissioning timeline is disclosed in the text routed to this domain. Note: the manufacturing-footprint block is truncated mid-name at 'Silvassa, D', so two of the five plant names and the mapping of three capacity figures to plants are not recoverable from this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management expects the Company to maintain stable growth, supported by its strong brand presence, extensive distribution network and sustained demand from the automotive segment
- Continued focus on premiumisation through synthetic and high-performance products is expected to support volumes and realisations
- Benefits of new channel-partner appointments, white-spot coverage and re-established mechanic/workshop relationships are expected to be visible in the next financial year
- A robust financial position characterised by low leverage and strong liquidity is described as providing resilience
- Indian GDP growth projected at 6.9% for FY 2026-27, with continued expansion in infrastructure, manufacturing and automotive supporting industrial demand
- Indian lubricants market valued at USD 4.92 billion in 2025 and forecast at USD 7.53 billion by 2034 (IMARC); automotive and transportation is the largest share at nearly 46%
- Global lubricants market valued at USD 178.98 billion in 2025, expected to reach USD 182.53 billion in 2026 and USD 213.93 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 2.0%, driven by synthetic and bio-based lubricants
- Premiumisation and the shift to synthetic products, driven by stricter emission norms and evolving OEM requirements, is stated to improve product mix and realisations across segments
- Rural and semi-urban lubricant usage remains subdued relative to rising vehicle ownership, leaving distribution and awareness expansion as a share-gain lever
- OEM partnerships offer long-term supply contracts, brand credibility and warranty-compliant demand
- EV adoption is creating demand for specialised coolants, lubricants and transmission fluids, while the existing ICE vehicle base remains substantial and sustains aftermarket demand
- Margin headwind: base-oil prices track crude and are exposed to geopolitical developments in oil-producing regions; competitive intensity and limited differentiation in some segments add pricing pressure
- Regulatory pressure (BS-VI in India, REACH and eco-label requirements globally) raises R&D and compliance investment while opening niche demand for biodegradable, low-toxicity products
- Industrial demand is tied to manufacturing, infrastructure and core sectors such as power, mining, construction and metals; India's industrialisation and government capital expenditure are expected to sustain it
- Selective rationalisation in the industrial lubricants business contributed to improved financial health while maintaining long-term customer relationships
- Overseas subsidiaries and the ENEOS VCL India joint venture contribute to consolidated turnover and profit alongside the standalone business
- Trade integration is expected to strengthen following the Free Trade Agreement with the European Union

The Company is re-establishing relationships with mechanics and independent workshops and expects the benefits of these initiatives to be visible in the next financial year.
The Board has decided to dissolve wholly owned subsidiary Veedol Deutschland GmbH, subject to compliances and clearances under applicable laws and regulations.

The next phase of manufacturing improvement will focus on reducing manual interventions through selective automation, optimising shift structures and workforce deployment, and enhancing consistency in output and productivity levels.

The Company will optimise existing manufacturing infrastructure through operational excellence, improved planning and productivity enhancement initiatives before undertaking any significant capacity expansion.
